speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):

I desire to say a few words with respect to this bill. Bills [DOT]Nos. 139, 140 and 141 all contain the same subject matter and are really collateral amendments effecting the main purpose which the government has in view, and I trust I will be excused if I make one statement with regard to the three of them. I think every member of this House will be in favour of any efficient measures which are taken to create public confidence throughout the country in the constitution and administration of the Supreme Court of Canada. I notice in the report of the Imperial conference that it is suggested-and in
fact the assent of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Justice to the recommendations of that report would seem to imply,-that, tentatively at least, they have agreed to the appointment of a sub-committee of the Imperial conference to inquire into, report upon and make recommendations with regard to amendments to certain imperial statutes, which give the statutory right to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to hear appeals from the appellate courts of the various provinces of Canada, and from the Supreme Court of Canada. A few years ago this parliament passed an amendment to the criminal code which now appears as section 1025. It provides that:
Nothwithstanding any royal prerogative, or anything contained in the Interpretation Act or in the Supreme Court Act, no appeal shall be brought in any criminal case from any judgment or order of any court in Canada to any court of appeal or authority, by which in the United Kingdom appeals or petitions to His Majesty in Council may be heard.
It was contended in this House at the time and subsequently in some of our courts that section 1025 did prevent the king in council from granting special leave to appeal in Canadian criminal cases. The constitutionality of the enactment recently came before the Privy Council in the ease of Nathan vs. the King, which is reported in 1926 appeal cases, page 482, and the Privy Council decided it was void ab initio. They declared that the ancient prerogative right of each citizen of the British Empire to appeal to the king in council had been embodied in certain statutory enactments of the Imperial parliament, notably the Judicial Committee Acts of 1833 and 1844, which expressly provided for the admission of any appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council from any judgments, sentences, decrees or orders of any court of justice within any British colony or possession abroad. Those acts also empowered the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, by sequestration of real and personal estate, goods, chattels and effects wheresoever lying within the dominions of His Majesty, to enforce obedience to orders of the Judicial Committee. I infer from the report of the Imperial Conference Committee that this government, at least as its views were expressed at the conference by the Prime Minister and by his colleague the Minister of Justice, contemplate amendment by the British parliament of those Judicial Committee Acts in such wise as to restrict, if not abolish entirely, the right of appeal from the Dominion courts to the king in council.

Simply because a few men become incapacitated at the early age of seventy-five, why should we provide that all men, no matter what their physical or mental capacity may be at that age, shall be retired from these high judicial positions? I find that another judge who has been sitting on the Supreme Court for nine years, a very estimable gentleman and a personal friend of mine for many years before he accepted his high position, will be seventy-three on September 30 next; two years more and that judge, right in his prime, will be compelled to retire on a pension. I find that another justice of the Supreme court who has served two years will, in seven years, be seventy-five years of age, and he will then be retired in like manner.
For my part, I think that in the retiring' of these two judges to whom I have referred we will be retiring a great portion of the judicial experience and intelligence now controlling the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada.
The bill also provides for the appointment of an extra judge. At .present six judges hold office; if I remember correctly five constitute a quorum, leaving one spare judge. Would it not be far better to restrict the number to six and to increase the salaries of the remaining judges? I know there is some hesitation on the part of certain members of the House to increase the salaries of those who hold high judicial positions, but the fact is that in the United States they pay higher salaries to the judges sitting on many of their state courts than we pay to the judges sitting on the Supreme Court of Canada. My ideal would ibe to have a Supreme court bench constituted of the very best legal intelligence that this country can produce, and I submit that the lawyers of Canada are not inferior in intelligence to the lawyers who plead before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council I Mr. Cahan.3

Appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada should be kept entirely non-political if possible. That is, the effort that is being made in this country. Sometimes we have made appointments that have been political in their character. That is true; both sides have done it. It has been the reward sometimes for candidates who have run elections. Men have run elections, gone into a campaign, faced a constituency and said:	Well, this is

But if we make the salaries, the emoluments and the pension that attaches to office adequate then with the realization that work well done for the state will be recognized not only by the state but by the community in which the judges live, we may be able to break diown slowly the pull and the pressure that comes from political considerations in appointments of this character and get our best minds on the bench.
What the 'hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said with respect to some men having done their best work at an advanced age is certainly very encouraging to one of my years, and1 I heard his observations with the greatest interest and pleasure, but I do sometimes think that when men have attained the age of seventy-five or eighty years there is a strain upon their mental powers in a country such as this that makes it undesirable for them to continue the administration of justice. I have held that view for a great many years. I do not say that seventy-five is the age; it is difficult to fix, because we have striking examples in every part of the country of men who at seventy-five and perhaps over have done their very best work. But these are the exceptions.
I should like further to say that it is not fair to institute a comparison between a judge in an older civilization and a judge in a country such as this. Judges in England are appointed from t'he barrister branch of the profession. They have had none of the drudgery of solicitors. Men in Canada who practise the profession usually practise both 
branches; they are both attorneys, solicitors and barristers, and if you appoint these men to the bench I think in most cases it will be found that before they reach the age of eighty there is a conscious or unconscious failing of t'heir mental powers. I do know that one distinguished member of the bar in this country declined judicial office because he said to me he felt that at his age-he had not attained eighty, but he was over seventy-he would not be able to discharge his duties in such a way as would be creditable either to himself or to the country. A former Minister of Justice declined to appoint to the bench anyone over seventy years of age, because he felt that it was improper to appoint to the bench anyone over that age, which may or may not have been correct. I do not desire to express a definite opinion with regard to the age, as between seventy-five or eighty, but I think you will find there is a general concensus of opinion among litigants in the country that when a judge has attained the age of seventy-five he has, not wishing to be unkind, outlived his usefulness. There are cases where this condition does not apply and there always will be such cases. But speaking generally when men have discharged the difficult duties and borne the wear and toil of professional work to the extent to which a successful practitioner does, at the age of seventy-five I think they should be willing to take a holiday and enjoy a well-earned pension. Whether seventy-five is the exact age or not, I am not prepared to say, but I do feel from my own observation that at the age of eighty no gentleman should be occupying a seat on the bench. That is my personal view.
Now with respect to this particular measure which will have the effect of retiring at once a member of the Supreme Court of Canada, I have had grave doubts in my own mind as to the soundness of legislation that terminates, in terms of age, a contract between the state and a judge which was not a condition of the contract when it was made. I mentioned my view to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice yesterday, because it will be remembered that under the British North America Act a judge is appointed during good behaviour or for life and when his commission is issued one of the terms of the commission is that very provision that he should hold office during good behaviour or life.
Now to add to that contract in reference to an existing judge a term whereby at the age of seventy-five he vacates office, or if he has already attained that age, he must vacate office, is really to create a breach of that contract by legislative authority, and

it may well be that the question, of compensation will be alleged to be involved, I, myself, presented that view to the Privy Council in connection with a icase that arose in the province of Alberta, and the court then held that it was competent for the appointing power to select, because of the terms of that particular legislation, without involving a breach of contract, a particular person to be chief justice of the court in question, although there had been a chief justice under the previous legislation. That was a matter arising under a particular statute. This parliament has power undoubtedly to pass this legislation. It has not power to limit the age of provincial judges, because it is provided in the statute itself that no limitation of age shall involve their removal from office. That is altogether different from the federal court. This parliament could, if it so desired, abolish the Supreme Court of Canada, it could abolish the Exchequer Court of Canada, and it could provide by reorganizing the constitution of the court, that no person could hold office after he reached the age of seventy-five, but that would involve the destruction of the court. What we are now doing involves a breach of the contract between the individual who holds office at the present time and the state, because his patent of office declares that he shall hold office during life or during good behaviour. He is still alive. His behaviour is not questioned, and the state has now said that because he attained the age of seventy-five years some time ago, he shall now forfeit or surrender his office-that by virtue of the statute his office is abolished, notwithstanding his patent. I suggested that it might be desirable to consider the question as to how far this parliament was committed under these circumstances to pay him during his lifetime the salary attaching to his office. I only mention that. I do not suggest it in any sense as being critical of the measure, but I suggest it because it is involved in the discussion of this matter. I think the minister should carefully consider that point. He was good enough to mention it to me yesterday and I have given some thought to the matter since.
May I say to my hon. friends to my left, do not imagine for a moment that those who belong to the legal profession urge large salaries and retiring allowances to the judiciary in order to advance their own interests. This is not a dose profession. It is a profession to which you will find, in the west particularly, that young men who have made their way by dint of toil and study have been attracted. It is important from the 32649-99
standpoint of the men who toil with their hands that there should be at all times in the country the utmost confidence in the courts of justice and confidence is begotten of a recognition and realization of knowledge, learning, ability and character. These attributes are of importance to judges. They are the instruments in the administration of justice. The essential quality of the Goddess of Justice is impartiality and justice is an attribute of God. If you are to have justice administered efficiently and faithfully, if you are to have confidence in the judges of our courts, to rely upon their judgments and to feel that the differences between labour and capital and the great issues involving property and men's liberties, privileges and lives are honestly and justly dealt with, it can be done only by attracting to the bench men with the qualifications and attributes to which I have alluded. It is for these reasons and not for any monetary consideration that those of us who have any hope and desire to attain judicial office do urge as strongly as we may that this high court of parliament should recognize that those who administer the law should be beyond suspicion and should be amply protected by sufficient salaries while they are able to discharge their duties and ample pensions when they are unable to do so.

We have had the doctrine stated in this House very clearly that you cannot possibly attract legal gentlemen enjoying a lucrative practice without offering very large salaries. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is a rather deplorable condition if such men when needed for the service of their country refuse to render that service except in return for eight, ten or fifteen thousand dollars a year. We were told during the war that every man was exjpected to devote his time to the service of his country for $1.10 a day. For the life of me I cannot quite see why the service required from privates during war time should be so very different from that which is supposed to be rendered by men of high moral ideals during peace time.
The member for West Calgary suggests it is essential that work to be well done should be well remunerated. I agree with that principle. But I would point out that that is not the principle commonly applied to the everyday affairs of life. For instance, the average wage paid in Canada is less than $1,000 a year. Will anyone say that with the cost of living what it is to-day $1,000, a year is an adequate sum on which a man can bring up a family? The evidence given before one of our parliamentary committees last session was to the effect that an annual income of $2,200 was necessary to maintain an ordinary family according to recognized Canadian standards.
Why is it that we are asked on the one hand to give these comparatively large salaries to a few individuals on the principle that otherwise we cannot possibly attract the right class of men, and on the other hand to allow large numbers of people to live below the standards of a decent subsistence? It is easily accounted for, of course-these poor people are driven to accept what they can get. They do not take up carpentering, railroading, farming or any other work because they are attracted to it, but because

Supreme Court Act
they cannot earn a living in any other way. It is quite possible that if the large salaries paid to lawyers could be cut down a little in the first instance some of them might be induced to become judges.
We are told that our judges have social and other obligations. Well, I have no objection to their trying to maintain as high a standard of' living as possible, but I would point out that there are large numbers of people in this country who have not even the means to secure the common necessities and amenities of life. It may be all very well for the judge to live in a highly restricted residential area; but on the other hand I would urge that the ordinary workingman ought to be assured at least a decent cottage, if you like, where he can live with his family in comfort and send his children to school. It is said that a great deal depends upon the proper dispensation of justice; but if children are forced at a tender age to go out on the street to earn a living because of the abominable conditions in their homes and the low standard of living there prevailing, why, I wculd say that we are pursuing a policy that inevitably will make work for our judiciary. If it is suggested that it might be a good thing to do away with some of these undesirable conditions immediately We are told that that would be paternalistic legislation. That term paternalistic always amuses me. If this proposal for judges' pensions is not paternalistic,-the caring for these poor gentlemen who have to maintain social and other obligations,-I do not know what it is.
It is further stated by the member for West Calgary that we ought to give good salaries in order that judges may overcome the temptations incident to their position, that otherwise they might be induced to accept bribes for the subversion of justice. Well, it is only two or three years ago since we revised the Bank Act, and at that time representations were made to us that the bank clerks were living on such small salaries that they were not even permitted to marry. And yet those clerks hold fairly responsible positions. I think we might then have passed legislation to enable those men to form an organization which would secure to them adequate salaries. But no, we could do nothing for them, even although we were told that some of them by reason of their meagre remuneration were tempted to commit acts of theft.	All I am asking for, Mr. Speaker,-and I am serious in this-is that we in this House should seek to legislate equally for the well-to-do and for the poor people of this country.
I cannot allow an opportunity of this kind to pass without urging that those of us who are trying to represent the common people and their interests must not permit legislation of this kind to go through without calling attention to the special pleas that have been advanced, and the principles that have been enunciated. I would say that when other cases come up these hon. gentlemen in ordinary fairness, ought to recognize that they should be decided according to the selfsame principles which they have been advocating in this chamber. It is of course quite understandable that if many lawyers receive emoluments amounting to $10,000, $20,000, $30,000, $40,000 or $50,000 a year, they would hesitate to take the smaller remuneration offered to judges. But that is only the beginning of the question. Again I would ask seriously why lawyers who are in what the labour men would call a union, a closed shop, should be permitted to receive such large salaries. I know it is very desirable that they shall maintain certain social standards and all the rest of it, but the point is that they are allowed to receive these large salaries and to maintain these social standards because of laws which are placed upon the statute books by this parliament and because of certain privileges which are granted to the legal profession in this country. I do not quarrel with them for trying to maintain high standards, but again I ask: Why should they unite with others to prevent other classes in the community from obtaining even the moderate standards which would quite satisfy most of them?
The hon. member for West Calgary made special reference to the men "who toil with their hands," and suggested that they ought to have a great deal of confidence in the judges. I am tempted for a moment to suggest that it is not by giving judges large salaries that you are likely to secure the confidence of those men who toil with their hands. One of the fundamental difficulties with laws to-day is the fact that those who make the laws, those who administer the laws, and those who sit on the bench are so far removed in their manner of life and indeed in their whole conception of life from the ordinary people that they are thereby almost disqualified from judging a case where on the one hand there is the ordinary man on the street to whom reference has been made, and on the other, the big corporation.

There are those who still urge that the employer ought to have a paternal relation to his employee, absolutely ignoring the fact that under modern conditions there is very little of the close personal touch that once existed between the employer and the employee. As Carlyle said many years ago, there is only a "cash nexus" uniting them. It must be recognized that under modem conditions a man passes from one occupation to another until before he has reached the age of sixty-five he has perhaps been in hundreds of different occupations. In the first place we must remember that since most of us were children the pioneer days have passed, and under modern competitive conditions it is not so easy as it was in the days of our childhood, for a man to make his way. It is a question of the condition of the market in relation to that particular matter and walk in life. That being so, there should be no objection raised to the payment of a reasonable salary to our judiciary. I submit that , our judges today are not paid what this Dominion of Canada can afford and what the Dominion' would be well justified in paying if it wanted to provide for the needs of the people in the best manner possible so far as their relations with the courts are concerned.

I do not entirely agree with
the hon. member who has just spoken. I do not say that it is a good thing to commercialize the position of the judges. In other words, I do not believe it is a question of supply and demand. I do not believe either that the people of Canada will censure this government for providing adequate salaries so that qualified and competent men will be members of the judiciary of Canada. I am not a lawyer and do not speak as a lawyer. The people themselves were quite content in years gone by with the judiciary and had
a great deal of confidence in the judges of Canada. I do not think that the question of salary will always bring to our services perhaps the men we desire, because occupation creates a desire as well as the salary. But there may come a limit to the salaries which we can offer in this country, and at the present time, for the salary mentioned, $15,000, I think we would be able to find many capable lawyers with all the qualities of a real first class high court judge who woulc} be willing to serve.
I listened attentively this afternoon to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and also to the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George combed all America and all Europe for very able men and women, keen of intellect and of great service to the community in which they lived, who had gone beyond the age limit. Our county court judges deal with minor cases, and when the act we recently passed becomes law it will apply to them. There ought to be no reflection on any man or woman in Canada on the score of age, but when we find that the minor court judges are required to retire from active service at the age of seventy-five, I think that provision ought surely in all fairness to apply to high court judges as well. We must all respect the judiciary of Canada, and we do. Fortunately or unfortunately we sometimes have to reflect on whether their appointment was by a Conservative government or a Liberal government, but I think in the Dominion of Canada we must congratulate ourselves on the high standing of our judges throughout the whole country and also in the Supreme Court of Canada at Ottawa. Many young men are coming forward in Canada who will be anxious to fill these positions which will be vacant before very long, and while I have no doubt the Minister of Justice will give every consideration to the suggestion made by his friends and also by those who sit on the opposite side, it is our desire and the desire of the country that the minister will take into consideration the appointment of lawyers of high standing in Canada, so that the judiciary may be respected, as we have had great respect for the judges throughout Canada in years past.

I have no objection whatever to the present bill. I have had to do in the past with the question of increases of salary of some of the judges. Public opinion in my province is that when a judge has served on the bench a term of years and becomes mentally and physically incapable of
Judges Act Amendment

further service he should be entitled to a pension. We have in the province of Quebec a number of judges who have taken up other occupations and are still in receipt of pensions from this government. That has occurred by virtue of certain laws enacted by this parliament and which we have discussed over and over again. I think when the Minister of Justice again takes up this subject he should provide that in the superior courts of Quebec a pension will be allowed to a judge only when he is physically or mentally unable to act, not to one in enjoyment of all his faculties and who retires in order to take up some other remunerative calling. That is the grievance of the people in my province, and I have heard it voiced on this floor. Indeed, we have such cases at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the condition my hon. friend refers to has been already met. In 1919 it was enacted:
That no annuity shall be granted to any judge under the provision of section 19 or 24 unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such judge should resign his office.
Prior to that, a judge after a certain length of service had the right to retire and receive his superannuation unconditionally. Now it is in the discretion of the governor in council either to grant or refuse such a request.
Is it open to a judge who retires to take up some other profession, such as a university professorship, at a salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he is still able to take up other work I think his request for retirement would be refused.

That is the abuse to which the people of my province object.
Sections 1 and 2 agreed to.

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78,. respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAT CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hour for private members' bills expired on Monday last, I had shortly reviewed the circumstances in connection with the incorporation of this company, and the various extensions that had

Georgian Bay Canal Company
been granted whereby it became possible for the company to continue in existence thirty years after its incorporation.
I had endeavoured to point out that the second reading of the bill affirmed the principle of the measure and that the principle affirmed by the House could not be varied in committee.
I had also endeavoured to point out that the granting of the -chanter involved the losing of large sums of money to this country in the way of annual rentals that might otherwise have gone to the exchequer. When we left that order of business I had 'been endeavouring to ask this House what was the principle of the measure under consideration, and I had not then concluded.
If hon. gentlemen are desirous of understanding what the principle of this measure
is,	it will only be necessary for them to look at the marginal note opposite section 1 of this bill, where they will find the words " Extension of time for commencement and completion ". Nothing is clearer than that unless some legislative action is taken by this parliament before the 1st day of May next, this company will have ceased to function. It will no longer be enabled to carry on its undertakings; it will no longer be a factor in the development of canals or water powers. If that be so, and I think you will admit that it is so, we have to ask ourselves, I submit, but a single question. We lawyers, about whom we heard something this afternoon, sometimes have a fashion of testing a problem by making certain inquiries with respect to
it.	I have an inquiry to address to hon. members in this House to-night, and it is this: would you in your place as a member of this House of Commons at this time-that is the year 1927-pass an act incorporating this company with the' powers indicated? That is the question. If you say yes to that, then you should vote for the second reading of the bill. If, in your conscience and by your reason, you could not say that in the light of the knowledge you now possess, you would rise in your place and vote to create a company wdth the powers that are given to this enterprise, then you should not vote for the second reading of the bill. Is that not fairly clear and obvious to everyone? Why? Because the bill-and I wish to bring it home to the minds of hon. members-divides itself into two separate and distinct undertakings; first, canals, and then power. If hon. gentlemen will look through the bill they will find that the principle of this proposed legislation -is: To enable this company, the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, hereinafter called the company, to commence
the construction of its canals, or any of them. That is the first. That is, that it may commence the construction of canals from the port of Montreal to Georgian bay, a distance of two hundred miles, through lakes, rivers and detours, and by the building of such canals make a waterway between those two points. That is the first branch of the undertaking. Go a step further, and we find the following:
-and subject to the provisions of this act, may, in connection with such construction and operation, exercise all the powers granted to the company by chapter 103 of the statutes of 1894 and amendments thereto.
And I read to this House the other evening, Sir, the section as placed in the act of incorporation when it was amended, by which the company was enabled to carry on its business as a power company. Therefore the powers of this company are divided -into two branches: (a) Its canal undertaking; (b) Its power undertaking; and the principle of the measure is to renew the life of, revivify and resuscitate a company whose life will expire on the first day of May next. Unless you are prepared, as members of -this House, to say that you would vote for the bill incorporating this company as it was in 1894 and subsequently amended, you should not vote for the revivification and resuscitation of the enterprise.
Let me go a step further. I am asked how I can establish that it is really intended that power should be the basis of this revivifying statute. - All I can say with reference to this is that apart from what was said by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) the other night, and to which I referred in answer to a question by the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), if my hon. friends will take the trouble to read the language of the memorandum submitted by the applicants for this legislation they will realize that it is alleged in terms that it is power they propose to develop, and it is by the sale of power that they propose to pay the cost of putting through this undertaking. They say:
Therefore the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal have the exclusive and overriding right to the use of water on the Ottawa river, a right which, when put into force, destroys all other claims. Any existing users of water in the Ottawa river are, to the extent to which they interfere with the right of development and control of that river for navigation, interlopers with no legal status whatsoever.
Therefore this House is asked now to revivify and resuscitate this enterprise, with the promoters alleging that any existing users of water in the Ottawa river are, to the extent to which they interfere with the right of de-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
velopment and control of that river by the company, interlopers with no legal status whatever.
I submit the Minister of Railways will hesitate before he will involve the country in that form of litigation. He says there are power rights on that river granted to other companies in days gone by. The promoters have brought before tihe House a memorandum in which they have stated that they are the overlords, and that nobody can be permitted to interfere with them on that river, and that if they do so they are interlopers without any legal status whatever. Is it the policy of the House of Commons to involve this country in litigation for tlhe purpose of having it declared, as the promoters have said, that they are the overlords upon that river? And this charter, in the language of these gentlemen, gives them supreme control over the Ottawa river, over two hundred miles of lakes and waterways, and they themselves allege that-it is not what I say in this House, it is what is alleged in tihe memorandum under which they seek this legislation-
By the special acts respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal company, the parliament of Canada has authorized that company to develop the navigation of the Ottawa river.
By so doing the parliament of Canada exhausted during the currency of these acts, the rights of the Dominion in regard to the granting of the use of water on the Ottawa river. Any executive authority granted by the Dominion for the use of water on the Ottawa river for any purpose except navigation and shipping is invalid as being ultra vires.
Therefore this company, that now seeks the sanction of parliamentary authority to breathe the breath of life after the first day of May next, alleges that this parliament has exhausted, during the currency of those acts, the rights of the Dominion in regard to the granting to anybody else of any powers whatever. Let there foe no misapprehension. Every hon. gentleman who gives the sanction of his vote and authority to this measure is stating his willingness to call into being a body, an entity, a corporation, with the authority and privileges and powers which the promoters say belong to their company. I ask any hon. gentleman on either side of the House if he will do it in face of that consideration.
In the face of thirty years experience, in the light of the knowledge we have gained, would any hon. member vote to call into being a company clothed with these powers, powers which I say they do not possess but which the promoters allege they possess? Why call into existence the canal company under these circumstances? There are two reasons why

we should not do it. It is not the policy of this country and has not been its policy to grant to a private enterprise the right to build canals and charge tolls. That is number one, and number two is that in view of our commitments with respect to railways and other means of transportation we cannot afford to lessen the revenues of our owi} enterprises.
And lastly we know that under the admin

istration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier nearly a million dollars was expended on surveys. I well recall when I first came to this House that Sir Robert Borden, yielding to the pressure put upon him with reference to this canal undertaking, granted the application for a royal commission. Investigations took place; the commission made reports and I say that nowhere in any report made upon this matter, nowhere in the notes of surveyors, will you find a single word that indicates that that enterprise may ever profitably or successfully function as a canal company. Then what are we doing? We are asked to give the breath of life to a dying enterprise that no single engineer says may be successful. We are asked to resuscitate a corporation that is dying, to which Sir Wilfrid Laurier gave its oongb, when the surveys were completed after spending nearly a million dollars, and of which we have not heard as a living enterprise since the days of the reports of the Sanford Evans commission. So none of us would give it power or life as a canal company for the reasons I have indicated.
How many hon. members would vote to give it being as a power company? Would any hon. members hand over 200 miles of lake and river waterway with the million and a quarter potential power development to a private enterprise without a single dollar return to this country? Where is my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) -he who did so -much for public ownership in the province of Ontario, he who lent his great power of intellect and the influence of his press to develop that enterprise in his province-where is he to-night? Does he say for a single moment that he would vote to give to this private corporation the authority to control 200 miles of waterway with the possible development of a million and a quarter horse-power without a dollar being .paid to this country?
I pointed out to this House the other evening that under the initial lease made by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1908 to Mr. Crawford Ross the country was to receive two dollars per horse-power. It was subsequently reduced when it was provided

Georgian Bay Canal Company
that the development should be greater. I observe that 25 cents was named by the solicitor for the new interests that took over the charter. But the rental was fixed at $50,000, to be increased to a higher figure.
If a full development of the million and a quarter horse-power on this 200 miles of lake and river waterway takes place the country is sacrificing not less than $500,000 per annum. Last Tuesday I put the loss at a quarter of a million dollars, but I find that figure is entirely too low. We get not a sou from the exploitation of these great natural resources.
I challenge any member to point to a single instance of the resources of this country having been alienated without some compensation. Not a dollar, not even a cent, is to be paid by those who are asking for a renewal of this charter, although those who had the lease in the early days were to pay two dollars per horse-power at Carillon. That is the position. Therefore I do submit with confidence, Sir, that there is not an hon. gentleman in this House who, if he had to consider this act of incorporation de novo, would at this date vote to create this canal or power company.
I said on Tuesday that I hoped my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) would be here this evening. I understand he is absent by reason of a social engagement, but perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) will consider the legal argument that I propose to submit to the House.

I thought that might
engage his attention for a moment. It has not been noted as a salient feature, but it is a matter of great importance to observe that three years after we became a confederation the parliament of Canada by chapter 24 of the statutes of 1870 passed an act declaring the Ottawa a navigable river, and that all works then existing or that might thereafter be built thereon should be works for the general advantage of Canada and should be subject to the exclusive power of the federal parliament. In 1898 we find a reference made to the supreme court as to the respective legislative powers of the Dominion and the provinces with regard to fisheries in navigable waters, and the Privy Council decided, Lord Herschell having delivered the judgment affirming the Supreme Court of Canada, that with respect to a river such as the Ottawa the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada extended to all matters, relating to the use of the waters for navigation and allied purposes. In fact, the Privy 32649-100

Council answered the questions submitted in the same sense as did the Supreme Court of Canada.
The matter is too familiar to members of this House for me to deal with it at length except to say that in the year 1925 the Privy Council had again to consider the whole question with respect to the ownership of navigable waters and of river and stream beds. Perhaps hon. gentlemen from Montreal will recall the decision in the Montreal harbour commissioners case. It was there decided-and I think it is very important that we should keep it in mind in this matter- by the law lords of the Privy Council that under the British North America Act the effect was to vest the harbour of Montreal as it existed in 1867 in the crown in the right of the Dominion; but to vest the bed and foreshore of the harbour in the crown in the right of the province. I find in the case, Montreal City vs. Montreal Harbour Commissioners, the principle is stated in these words at page 311 of the appeal cases for 1926:
Under section 91 exclusive legislative authority is given to the Dominion parliament in the matters of navigation and shipping. Under section 92, head 10, lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting a province with any other province, or extending beyond the limits of a province, lines of steamships between a province and any British or foreign country, and such works as although -wholly within a province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more provinces, are all taken out of the legislative authority of the provinces and placed (by section 91, head 29) exclusively under that of the Dominion parliament.
Then the judgment proceeds:
But the question remains whether section 91, head 10, of the act, which empowered the Dominion parliament to legislate as to navigation and shipping, empowered that parliament to authorize the extensive works undertaken by the commissioners on the banks and foreshore and in the bed of the river. In considering this question it is necessary to bear in mind the nature of those works. They include, not only dredging operations, but an embankment and railway on the shore of the river, quays, a dry dock and ship repairing plant, and it would appear to be impossible that works of this character and extent could be constructed and used without an exclusive occupation of the soil equivalent to possession. Now there is no doubt that the power to control navigation and shipping conferred on the Dominion by section 91 is to be widely construed. As was pointed out by Lord Herschell in the judgment which he delivered on behalf of the board in Attorney-General for the Dominion v. Attorney-General for the provinces-namely, the first of the three Fisheries cases-the terms on which those powers are given are so wide as to be capable of allowing the Dominion parliament to restrict

Georgian Bay Canal Company
very seriously the exercise of proprietary rights in a fashion which, to a great extent, depends on the discretion of that parliament. What was said in that case about the enactment of regulations and restrictions in matters relating to fisheries being excluded from the competence of the provincial legislatures applies not less to matters relating to navigation and shipping. But while this is so, it does not appear to their Lordships that the right of the Dominion extends so as to authorize them to vest in a body like the commissioners an exclusive right to occupy property of the province without compensation and to erect upon it permanent works, such as quays, docks and railways.
There we have the last authoritative statement in respect of the matter. As was pointed out by Lord Herschell in the first of the three fisheries cases, the exercise of legislative power is one thing, the exercise of a proprietary right is another; and the proprietary right in respect of the river bed of the Ottawa, which is a navigable stream, declared so by parliament, is vested in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario and not in this parliament. I want to point out a very significant thing, because it is of the utmost importance that in considering-
What does the hon. member think of the Maclaren case which was decided by the Privy Council in the early nineties?

That case is not at all
in keeping with this. The ease I am referring to was decided, as my hon. friend probably knows, in the closing days of 1925 and is reported in the 1926 appeal cases. It determines definitely, until legislation to the contrary is passed, that the legislative power regarding navigation and canals resides in this parliament, but that the proprietary right to the bed of the river and the foreshore is with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

My friend knows that in
the Maclaren case the Privy Council decided that the bed of the Ottawa river belonged to the riparian owners to the medium Slum aquae.

I held no brief such
as the hon. member has mentioned. I did not use the brief which the hon. member has mentioned nor any of the arguments to be found in it.

The word "brief'' was
used by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I did not use the word in any offensive sense. The hon. member for Bow River stated that the document had been given to him by the hon. member for Ottawa, and it was placed on Hansard in that way.

With the legal learning
which the hon. gentleman has he will understand that it has no binding effect on my argument.

I did not suggest that
it bound my hon. friend. I suggested only that it should bind the promoters.
Let me go a step further in this citation. The present Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) intervened, saying:
Mr. Forke: The minister's statement is simply an explanation; it does not alter anything?
Mr. Graham: Matters stand just as they did before.
Mr. Caldwell: How much development has taken place under this bill?
Mr. Graham: So far as I know, there has been just the preparation of plans.
Mr. Ryckman: What rights are maintained or contended for by the government?
Mr. Graham: No rights which the federal government has ever had are being interfered with by the extension of the charter. If my hon. friend wants me to go into a discussion of the question as between federal and provincial rights I am afraid I shall have a considerable task.
There it ended. That was the last extension. Since then, with the decision of the Privy Council in the Montreal harbour commissioners' case, can this House, in view of the contention made by the promoters of this measure, give its consent to the second reading? Can the Minister of Immigration, in the light of the very pertinent inquiry which he then made, do so? Can the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Euler), under those circumstances, do so? I venture to hope not.
I leave that matter with the House with one additional fact not referred to at that time by the then Minister of Railways, namely, that in 1870 the Ottawa river, with all improvements, past, present and future were declared works for the general advantage of Canada. In the light of those facts, how can this House treat this as a private bill?
In view of my desire to conclude what I have to say, I will refer to only one more matter. Should this House pass legislation, should it give its assent to the principle of a measure such as this, should it send to committee a bill which invites litigation against the Dominion? In terms the bill does that. Why? Because from information given to us the other evening by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) and from the three sessional papers to which I have already referred, we now know there are rival power interests contending for rights in the Ottawa river. We now know there is a rival power company which contends it has large rights upon that river. We know further, that those rights expire on the first day of May of this year. The Minister of Railways alleged that this was done practically for the purpose of having them synchronize. Unless this parliament intervenes, the rights of this canal and power enterprise expire on the first day of May and the rights and privileges of this

Georgian Bay Canal Company
private power company also expire on the first day of May. What then is the duty of parliament? Far be it from me to suggest what that duty should be for others. What is my duty? My duty is, so far as my vote and voice are concerned, to see to it that this parliament gives no new life to an enterprise that we would not in this day create if we were called upon to do so, and that we leave the river Ottawa free, by permitting this charter to lapse and by refusing to renew the license to the private company, reserving the vested rights of the owners of the 250 horsepower development.
The hon. member for Bow River this afternoon asked the Minister of Railways what he proposed to do, and the minister said that he was waiting for this bill to go to committee. The minister in his speech the other night had the hardihood to suggest to this House that the matter could all be threshed out there. He knew, or he should know, that the only thing that can be dealt with in that committee is the right of this company to a renewal of this charter. That is the principle of this measure. Therefore the committee could not there deal with the extension of the lease of a private enterprise, which lease has been extended to the first day of May next.
I know not what may be the duty of each individual member to his own mind, reason and conscience, but I know what my duty is. I know it is my duty on this occasion to vote not to send the bill to committee; to declare that it is, as it is indeed, a public measure fraught with the gravest possibilities of danger to the public interest and bringing no revenue to this country. I know it is my duty to say, so far as my vote, and voice are concerned, that this company has had its day and ceased to be; that this company shall not be revived; that it shall not foe resuscitated; that it shall not foe a menace to the government of this country by preventing the bringing of revenue to the exchequer from the development of power on the Ottawa river.
But I do not stop there. We know that a small company with a development of 250 horse-power was licensed, and that that 250 horse-power development with one wheel may possibly be extended to 650 horse-power if desired. Let us instruct our Minister of Railways-if necessary I am prepared to move a resolution to this effect-that this House is resolved that this lease shall not be extended beyond the first day of May. Then what happens? We then leave the Ottawa river free; we leave the province of Ontario with its rights to the soil to the middle of the stream to deal with the situation as it pleases,
I Mr. Bennett.]
to make arrangements with the Dominion government and with the government of Quebec for the development of electric energy. We leave the province of Quebec free to deal with its share of the soil under that stream as it pleases, to license private enterprise if it so desires or to provide for public development. We leave the two provinces free to pursue the course they desire as their interests may determine; we leave provincial rights untouched; we leave the right of this Dominion untouched, and we save to the people of Canada 200 miles of river and lake waterway with a million and a quarter horse-power of electrical energy, the revenue from which will come to the country. In times past we have leased these powers as we have developed our railways and canals, and they have brought much money to the exchequer of the country. Now we have a chance which rarely comes in the life time of men; this parliament, in the plenary exercise of its authority has the right to say, "We will not again call into being this enterprise; we will let it die the death it has merited, die from inanition, die because for thirty years it has done nothing, and because for that long period, more than half the life of this confederation, it has not exercised its functions, its powers and its privileges." We have an opportunity to say, "We will give you no new lease of life in the light of the knowledge we now possess."
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been silent. This is not a political matter; there are men of the Liberal faith who are stronger supporters of the doctrine of public ownership than any man on this side of the House, even any man to my immediate left. My friend the Minister of Customs is 6ne. The great province of Ontario which now has nearly $300,000,000 invested in hydro-electric enterprises-provincial, municipal and civic-[DOT] contains many men who are earnest supporters of public ownership. Through ill repute and good my friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) has given the great undertaking the assistance of his pen, his mind and his voice, and he is a Liberal. I have not been noted for my strong advocacy of public ownership but, Sir, this is mor* than that; it far transcends that principle. The question is whether or not I shall vote to hand over to private interests 200 miles of waterways and a million and a quarter horsepower of electrical energy without a dollar of compensation to the people of this country whether I shall invite the possibility of litigation between Quebec, Ontario and this Dominion. The time has now come when for the first time these two things synchronize; we have the expiration of the lease and the

Georgian Bay Canal Company
disappearance of the company; let them die the death together.
One word more, Sir, and I have concluded. It has been said that we on this side of the House among others have during all these years voted for the renewal of this charter without making a protest. I have shown that that is not quite so; I have shown that there were members alive to the importance of this matter in 1924 and that my good friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) was alive to its importance although it was not a matter affecting western communities. But, Sir, this is the thought I would leave with the House. Shall we blindly follow what we have done in days gone by or, in the light of wider knowledge and new experiences, mark out a new place upon the statute books? That is the question. Shall! we be statesmen or politicians? Shall we be placemen or legislators? Which shall we be? I cannot conclude better than with words which have been ringing in my ears during the last few days as I have been thinking of this question, the words of a great American poet who, in the light of knowledge and experience said:
New occasions teach new duties: Time makes ancient good uncouth;
They must upward still, and onward, who -would keep abreast of truth.

I think I understand the meaning of the resolution, but perhaps the minister	had	better	give	us a	word of
explanation.

There is at the present time no workmen's compensation board in the province of Prince Edward Island. Government employees under the legislation now existing	are	dealt	with	by	provincial
machinery in the other provinces, and it is desirable to create in some manner machinery which will deal with injured government employees in Prince Edward Island. The government of that province does not intend to set up any workmen's compensation board, and this amendment to the act is designed to make the same scale and terms of compensation apply as would be the case if the employee were a native of New Brunswick instead of Prince Edward Island. So far as the machinery of operation is concerned, it

is intended to work through the machinery of the government of Prince Edward Island. I shall be glad to furnish particulars as to the details of cooperation with the government of the island in this matter on the second reading of the bill.
Have the employees asked for this?
Yes, for many years.

Are these Dominion
government employees?

Yes.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concuned in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 227, to amend an act to provide compensation where employees of His Majesty are killed or suffer injuries while performing their duties.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:

Will the minister explain
this measure?

This bill is a very short but a very important one. It provides for the regulation of the export and grading of fruit in the same manner as cheese and butter are graded for export. For the last two years an inspector has been employed voluntarily by the fruit men at the various points to do the inspecting. An inspector was appointed in British Columbia and the result was very satisfactory, so much so that a large proportion of British Columbia fruit has either gone into the interprovincial trade or has been exported under government certificate. I think a very large percentage of the fruit has gone forward under government inspection. The province of Ontario has adopted a system of government inspection, and the maritime provinces have come to the conclusion that if they were to get the best results with their export fruit they would have

Live Stock Act
to make provision for the inspection. This bill provides for such inspection. The inspection has been done voluntarily for two years in the same way as we inspect our grain for export and our butter and cheese for export.	.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Motherwell thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 228, to amend The Fruit Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

When shall the bill be
read the second time?

Go ahead.
Mr. MOTHERWELL moved the second reading of the bill.

The bill has not been
printed and distributed. I object to it.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .

speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, 1923, and to make further provisions, as to membership in live stock exchanges, the inclusion of cooperative associations, the rules, regulations and by-laws to be applicable to such exchanges, and penalties for violation of the act.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext:
Has the bill been before
the committee on agriculture, and have they adopted the resolution?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext: The resolution has not been before the committee on agriculture, but the bill will go there.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext:
I would like an
explanation of the resolution.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext:
As a result of certain differences that arose last spring between one of the live stock exchanges and a cooperative marketing association, it was drawn to the attention of the department that no provision was made for the cooperative marketing of live stock. It is true there was no special mention of the cooperative associations, because since the act was first drafted and since it got its last revision in 1923 the
cooperative marketing of live stock has come into such prominence that probably from fifty to sixty per cent of the live stock that is marketed and delivered at our exchanges comes through cooperative sources. In addition to that the act has grown obsolete in some other respects; consequently it has been decided to make a general amendment of the act by giving more recognition to cooperative associations and giving the producers their representative on the exchanges through the live stock associations, introducing provisions that would give more control to the exchanges themselves, and also making certain provisions in regard to penalties. The bill is printed and I expect it will be on the files on Monday morning. On the second reading I propose to ask that the bill be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization, and every oportunity will be given for all interests to be heard.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext: Was a conference held between the various live stock exchanges before the bill was printed? I understood the conference was to take place and all parties given a chance to express their views.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext: Yes. In order to get at the will of the people as nearly as possible with regard to this important question, a conference of the cooperative live stock associations was held, and representatives of the agricultural departments of the four western provinces and all other parties interested in the question of live stock selling was held in the city of Regina on the 17th and 18th of February. A conference was also held of representatives of the five eastern provinces in the city of Ottawa on the 2nd day of March, composed of representatives from similar bodies-provincial departments of agriculture, the eastern live stock union and all other bodies interested in this matter were represented. The views and conclusions of each body were reconciled as far as it was humanly possible so to reconcile them. Their differences were ironed out and the results are embodied in this bill.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext: Have the various societies had an opportunity of reading this bill?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .
speechtext:
The purpose of this resolution is merely a warning that the bill is coming. I cannot very well give my hon. friend the contents of the bill, but it provides for what I have indicated-recognition of the principle of cooperative marketing, more control of exchanges, certain penalties for infractions, and so on.
Special War Revenue Act

speechtext: Is not this the act concerning which there was a legal decision last year throwing some doubt upon its validity as applied to the provinces?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT, 1923, AMENDMENT .

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Superannuation Act, 1924, and to make such further provisions respecting allowances, benefits and contributions as may be deemed necessary for a better administration of the act.	.
Motion agreed to and the House went into _ committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I want
to ask the minister if the bill which he proposes to base on this resolution makes any provision for temporary employees. There are a large number of temporary employees in the service, and for the last two years in particular I have brought to the attention of the government from time to time the anxiety and desire of these temporary employees to be made permanent. Many of them have been in the service for several years, and yet they are unable to secure the benefits accruing to permanent employees. If they are not covered, I would ask the minister to consider making provision for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should not
like to make a commitment as to incorporating the temporary employees in this act without having some more information before me from the superintendent of insurance. I am not sure whether my hon. friend means temporary employees who have been in some of the regular departments for many years or temporary employees who are in certain branches that for a time it was considered were temporary. I know the superintendent of insurance has this matter under consideration and when the bill comes down we might be in a better position to discuss the matter. As my hon. friend knows, the Superannuation Act was passed three years ago. In the administration a number of defects have been

Civil Service, Superannuationa Act
brought to the attention of the Department of Finance which is charged with the administration of the act. The amendments contained in the draft bill are for the purpose of removing these defects and making the act better serve the conditions it was designed to meet. Incidentally I may say to my hon. friend that I think it extends the period of election to July, 1927." That was in the bill as presented last year.

I refer not to men who are hired by the day for odd jobs, but to employees who are classified as temporary but who are really just as permanent as others except that they do not receive these benefits.
I hold under my hand a communication from Mr. Knowles, National President of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada, and I will read a clause or two which will indicate the condition which, I think, is one that should be rectified:
Following up our communication regarding the "temporary employee" problem we are submitting the case for permanent appointment of the employees of the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment.
With few exceptions the majority of the staff have served from seven to nine years with the department, and in a large number of cases the civil service appointment was made immediately after discharge from war service, others are indirect victims of war service, thus further adding to the term of public service.
Practically every male member of the staff is a returned soldier of good record, as for the female employees, many have served overseas, while others are indirectly victims of war service brought about by a loss of near relatives in war areas.
And so on. Then there is another group. This is in another communication from the same gentleman:
Cleaners in public buildings with fifteen years' service are classified as temporaries and others doing the same class of work in the same building with less than two years of service are classified as permanent.
Thus we have employees who have been for many years in the service still carrying on as temporaries, while others in the same building and doing the same class of work are on the permanent list and enjoying or having the prospect of enjoying the privileges that accrue to permanent employees. There are other cases: for instance all the employees in the Income Tax branch who have for many years been asking to be recognized as permanent employees. I am not at the moment arguing with regard to appointment by the civil service. What I am asking is that these employees, who are obviously regular employees of the government as much as any others who are ranked as permanent, should enjoy the same privileges and* advantages as
their fellow employees enjoy. That in a nutshell is my point and frankly I think this condition ought to be rectified. For the last three years and prior to that, but particularly during the last three years, they have been asking very urgently for this redress; they have been waiting from time to time, assured that redress would in all probability be afforded w'hen certain consideration was given to the various acts affecting this. I am informed by these officials that they have during the last few weeks been anxiously awaiting the introduction of this legislation expecting that their grievances will be remedied under it. I would take this opportunity of urging the minister to make provision in this bill to take care of these various classes of temporary employees.

This is an opportune time for the Minister of Finance to take this matter under consideration, and, in connection with the legislation now proposed to introduce a measure which will make permanent employees who have had a long service not only in the public departments but in branches mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and service overseas for a period of years preceding their service in the branches. Some of these men have now been serving the country for thirteen years. This matter has been brought repeatedly to the attention of the govern' ment. I myself have brought it to the attention of the government on at least three occasions this year and each time I have received an assurance that the matter was under consideration. Furthermore, on one occasion, I am not sure in what year, this matter was dealt with by order in council so that the claims of the cases referred to were in that way recognized.
One class not referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver is that of employees in the Soldier Settlement Board, who are to-day, I believe, carrying on work in connection with the empire settlement scheme. This is clearly not a temporary work such as the soldier settlement scheme might have been considered. They are being used now for the general work in connection with immigration, a very important work. The claims of these men should be recognized; they should be put on the same basis as other members of the civil service. I hope when this bill is introduced the minister will have dealt with these claims. It is not a difficult matter because it has been investigated before, and the claims have been recognized. I feel certain it is a simple matter to deal justly with them at this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When hon. gentlemen have the bill before them they will be in a better position to discuss the whole bill.

Will the bill to be founded upon this resolution take care of the promise made by the Prime Minister the other evening as to the extension of time which employees in certain departments would be given for election?
