Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved that the House go into committee to considered the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the provisions of the Pension Act relating to the Federal Appeal Board, and to designate the number of members of which the board shall consist, the duration of their term of office, and their eligibility for reappointment.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Would the minister be
good enough to explain the purpose of this resolution?

This resolution,
and the bill to be founded on it will permit of the reappointment of some of the Federal Appeal Board commissioners in order that they may continue their work. There is this further change: whereas the act to-day reads that there shall be from five to seven members, it is proposed under the bill that there shall be three to seven members, thus permitting the government to reduce the number if they find it necessary to do so.

Are these appointments
at the present time only temporary?

The last amendment to the act gave the government the right to make appointments for two years. That period will expire this season, and it is now proposed to extend the time or to grant power to reappoint if necessary.

Is the government reducing the number to three instead of five?
Mr, KING (Kootenay); It will be in the government's power to do so, if the legislation passes, but it will be dependent upon the amount of work to be done. As it is now the membership may be five to seven; we are taking the right to make it three to seven. The number will probably be lessened if and when the work gets less.

For how many years are
the members of the board to be appointed?

In the bill the
period proposed is five years. It will be within the power of the government at any rate to fix a time within this period. We think it better to have a fixed term rather than to be bringing in amendments every second year.

There is no idea of
changing the personnel of the board?

This is an opportune time
to interrogate the minister in regard to some question which I placed on the order paper at least ten days or two weeks ago-to be precise, on March 9. Those questions read:
1.	Will legislation be introduced at this session of parliament providing relief for disabled and partially disabled war veterans at present excluded from pension benefits owing to the existing regulations?	'
2.	When will the bill be introduced for the said purpose?
Now the minister has had ample opportunity to reply to these questions, and seeing that the matter involved is one of very great importance to returned men who have been unable to qualify under the present regulations, I should like to ask the minister what he has to say about it. I should like the minister to intimate, if it is possible for him to do so, that he is prepared to bring down legislation to provide for these men who are unable to carry on and to look after themselves. They should be well provided for, in view of their services at the front.

I must apologize to my hon. friend and to the House for not answering his questions earlier. An answer was prepared but it was not sufficiently direct and on that account I withheld it. I hope to give my hon. friend a reply within the next day or two.

Is it not a fact that at the present time it takes almost a year to get a case before the appeal board, and is not that delay due to the fact that the board has to cope with such a volume of work?
Pension Act Amendment
I did not hear my hon. friend's question.

Is it not a fact that it requires almost a year for the appeal board to dispose of a case, for the reason that there are so many other cases awaiting decision? Yet this resolution proposes to reduce the number of members of the appeal board at the government's discretion, and that, apparently, will create further delay.

No, I think not. It will be within the discretion of the government to reduce the number of members if they find .the work is slackening off. There are many appeals yet to be heard, and the desire of the government now is to make it possible to reappoint the members of the board in order that the work may go on. If later it is found that the work is lessening and that it would be desirable to reduce the number of members, it will be within the power of the government to do so.

Are you not in receipt of complaints to-day that these appeals are just about one year behind? Have not representations to that effect been made to the minister? If that is true, and if you reduce the number of members of the board, it will mean that there will be that much longer delay.

We do not propose to reduce the number now; we are taking power to do that in the event of the work slackening. What we have in mind is that the work shall be properly carried on. As to the number of appeals coming before the board, my hon. friend will admit, I think, that the task they have is a very difficult one. They can only accomplish so much work and the cases coming before them must be dealt with in turn. I understand the board are travelling east and west trying to overtake the work entrusted to them with a view to cleaning up, but in view of the number of appeals it will take some time to do that.

There is just one point upon which I should like to ask the minister for information. Some little time ago a case was brought to my notice in which it was proposed to apply for an appeal. This case will be heard in western Canada, Now I was notified by one of the officials of the appeal board that when the board reaches this particular point in western Canada in the spring, some time in April or May, no more appeals will be accepted for the present. That will mean that this particular appeal will not be heard until a year later. Is that the method 
of transacting business followed by the board? Is it not possible to arrange that they shall hear all pending appeals from that particular point when they get there this spring?

I am not familiar with the case my hon. friend speaks of, but I shall be very glad to bring it to the attention of the chairman of the board. I think when the board go west they should try to clear up all the cases that have been presented to them.

I merely make the
suggestion that when the appeal board is sitting in any particular district it should stay there long enough to clean up all these appeals.
I think so.

It is a waste of time
and a great inconvenience to men appealing to have their cases put off for another twelve months.

What is the minister's
information as to the real necessity for this board? That is to say, are there many findings of the pension commissioners that are found, upon appeal, to be unjust to the soldiers, in the view of the appeal board?

I have not t'he
figures before me that would give the information for which my hon. friend asks; I did not know the resolution was coming up tonight. But when the bill comes up for second reading I shall have the figures here, and' I think it will be shown that the creation of the appeal board has been justified; they have heard many cases. Some have been consented to and in other cases the judgment has confirmed the decision of the pension board. In the majority of cases the decision of the pension board has been confirmed, but in other cases a contrary finding has been brought in. Taking everything into consideration we think the creation of the appeal board has been justified and that they have performed a useful service.

On what particular
grounds are most of the appeals based? Is there any regulation covering the matter?

I understand that
the soldier who has been refused a pension by the pension board on the grounds of non-attribuitability to service may appeal to the appeal board, and many cases have been appealed.

I had a case before the
board a few years ago where the appeal board-I am speaking from memory-found

Pension Act Amendment
an aggravated disability, but could not award any pension because the primary board had stated that there was no disability. It seems to me that that is an anomaly in the act that should be corrected, and I would like to hear from the minister in regard to it.

I think there are
difficulties there. Generally speaking I think these appeals are being taken and in the majority of cases, in fact, in practically every case, the appeal is sustained and a pension awarded. But in some cases there has been disagreement between the pension board and the appeal board, and such cases are allowed to stand.

It would seem to me
that in that case the main purpose of the appeal 'board is defeated. A man makes application to the pension board for a pension, he is refused, and he appeals to the appeal board, and although they find that he is entitled to a pension he cannot receive one owing to the previous decision of the primary board. Does not that seem ridiculous?
Is this seven-year limitation a cast iron rule so far as disability is concerned?
Yes, according to the act to-day.

Does the lodging of an
appeal entail any cost?
I think not.

I should like to ask the
minister again in regard to a question I have had standing on the order paper since March 9th, reading as follows:
1.	Will legislation be introduced at this session of parliament providing relief for disabled and partially disabled war veterans at present excluded from pension benefits owing to existing regulations?
2.	If so, when will the hill be introduced for the said purpose?
I would ask the minister whether or not he intends to bring down this legislation at the present session. He is throughly aware that hundreds of cases are not provided fot under the present regulations. These men cannot possibly qualify for pensions under the present regulations, and I think it is up to the minister to let me have a reply to this question which I have had standing on the order paper for over two weeks. I would like some satisfaction. The minister has had hundreds and hundreds of complaints with regard to this matter. He must be in a position to size up the situation and I would like
to know whether he will or will not bring down legislation at this session to provide for cases of this kind. I want a direct answer, yes or no.

Mr. Chairman,
the question will be answered in accordance with the usual procedure.
That is no satisfaction.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a case that is more or less individual, but there are many such in Canada to-day. I refer to those returned soldiers who are debarred by the statute of limitations from obtaining a pension. After they came back from the war they did not apply for a pension for a period of years and when they did apply it was too late.
I realize that if the law were left wide open, many would apply who might not deserve a pension; nevertheless these men to whom I refer were 'big enough and patriotic enough to join the colours when the country needed them, and because they did not apply for a pension within a certain period after their return, to-day some of them although incapable of working, are outside relief. I know of a case or two where a returned soldier is dependent on the charity of the provincial government and is an inmate of a convalescent home. Those men are there, dependent on charity, simply because they did not ask for a pension within the time required. They are there as the result of their war service, but they are absolutely outside the pale of any consideration under the present law. I do not blame the government because I believe in the statute of limitations, but I do say that in this year of our diamond jubilee these particular cases should be considered. Some of these returned men to-day are physically unable to carry on even the common functions of life. Surely the government should listen with respect to the advice of the medical authorities who vouch for these cases and provide some relief for these deserving men. I appeal to the minister to give this matter his most serious consideration, and see if relief cannot be provided this session for these cases that are debarred otherwise from relief.

I think I am entitled to an answer from the minister, and I think I am entitled to an answer, yes or no. Does the minister propose to do something at this session, or does he not? He is thoroughly familiar with the situation. He knows that there are hundreds of returned men in Canada to-day who are not fit to carry on, but who cannot qualify for a pension under the
Pension Act Amendment

present regulations. The minister cannot have escaped considering this situation, because he has had hundreds of applications for a pension from these men. That is admitted, and I think it is our duty to make provision for such cases at this session. I again appeal to the minister to give me a yes or no answer as to whether he proposes to bring down the necessary legislation at this session to see that these cases are adequately provided for. We are entitled to the information; it is due not only to myself, but to the country.
I can only say, Mr. Chairman, that the question will be answered in the usual course when questions are called.

I think the question
asked by the hon. member is a fair one. We are getting within reasonable distance of the end of the session. It is quite possible that we shall be out of here in three weeks, and I hope we will. That being so, it seems to me the government might well tell us what legislation they are going to bring down. We are dealing with the question of pensions and I think it is only fair that the question should be answered. The minister knows whether he is going to bring down any legislation this year to modify the Pensions Act. If he is not going to introduce further legislation he can give a straight answer, and I think we should not have to wait for the answer to the question on the order paper.

The matter has
been and is still under consideration, and I am not in a position to state to-night what legislation will be brought down. The answer prepared by the department was not satisfactory; I considered it evasive, and I preferred to make a direct answer. I apologize to my hon. friend for not having an answer, but as I say, there will be a direct answer when questions are called. I thought that to-night the resolution would be accepted. It deals more or less with the appeal board and the question whether their term should be extended. If it is desired that the Pension Act be discussed on the second reading of the bill, well and good. I rather thought that when the estimates of the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment w7ere before the House there would be an opportunity of discussing the matter of legislation regarding pensions. My hon. friend from Skeena a few moments ago suggested that we should do more than we are doing.	I think if
he would get in touch with the pension commissioners and the officers of the depart-
ment he might obtain some information. Although there is a limitation of seven years, many cases are being dealt with to-day; the files of the soldier, or indirect evidence, are being considered, and many cases are brought before the board. Whether or not the period of seven years should be extended is a matter that I think should be discussed later, and I shall foe glad to discuss it.
When questions are called, probably on Monday next, the minister will give an answer?
I think so.
Will the question of the limitation of seven years foe up for discussion before the session closes?

Yes, on supply
perhaps, or on the second reading.
Mr. MILLAR [DOT] Has the pension board the right to go beyond the seven years?

Yes. If evidence is adduced before the pension board that the soldier had disability during service-and his file will show that, that would be considered as an application as of date of entry on the file. Some of these cases are difficult and possibly slow in development, but many of them are being dealt with.

Seeing that the minister is making provision to decrease if necessary the personnel of the appeal board, why has it 'been found necessary in the last six months to increase the personnel of the Board of Pension Commissioners? Why is it, when probably the peak of work in connection with the work of pensions has been passed, that the minister has found it necessary in the last six months to add to that board by order in council? I am not criticizing the appointment, but why was it necesary?

There is no intention at the present time to reduce the number of members of the appeal board, but in bringing in the legislation extending the period for five years we hope that in the course of three or four years their work will be pretty well concluded, and it may be possible to reduce the number. The suggestion comes from the chairman that the reduction might be made if the work should justify it. In regard to increasing the number of members of the pension board, it is true that an order in council was passed providing that one of the members of the service, a medical man, should sit in with the board and form a quorum. The board have found it necessary to do some travelling, and they sug-

Pension Act Amendment
gested that Dr. Keyes be made a member of the board in order that they might have a quorum if they were travelling outside of Ottawa. There has been no increase in the staff as far as that is concerned.
I cannot see that it is a sufficient reason for increasing the personnel of the board seven or eight years after the war, especially when the great bulk of the work has been done.
I wish it were.

I know my hon. friend wants to be fair. The addition to the board has not increased the expenditure in any way. The officer who is serving at the suggestion of the chairman and members of the board is in the service as a medical officer and there has been no increase in the salary paid to him. It is merely to facilitate the business of the board that he may sit in and form a quorum when necessary.

I do not want to be understood as criticizing the appointment or the salary. But is it not a fact that members of the Board of Pension Commissioners are paid higher salaries than medical men in the service?
I think so.
Then you increase the expense.
No.
Then you were not fair to the appointee.
This gentleman is merely filling in to form a quorum when necessary. There is no increase in salary; it is merely to facilitate the work of the beard and has been done at the request of the board.

I am getting further at
sea all the time. He is either a member of the board of commissioners or he is not. If he is he ought to receive the same salary as the others.

He is not a member of the board. I will be very glad to lay the order in council on the table, so that my hon. friend will understand it. There are times when a quorum is required. This gentleman is thoroughly familiar with the work and it is necessary that they should have a quorum in order to make a decision. He fills in on such occasions and acts in that capacity:
Then he is not permanent?
He is not considered permanent.

Will the minister be prepared when he brings in this bill to discuss the handicaps under which the Federal Appeal Board operates? Let me recount one of them. The Federal Appeal Board cannot change the diagnosis of the pension board, and upon that depends whether or not the ex-service man receives a pension. I contend that the appeal board should be able to decide the diagnosis just as well as the pension board.

I shall be very glad to have a discussion on that when the bill is before the House for second reading or on the estimates of the department. I think the discussion would be useful, for an important principle is involved.

That is the very point I brought up. I can cite the minister a case where the Board of Pension Commissioners found no disability-I am not saying whether they were right or wrong-but the appeal board found there was disability. However, they could do nothing. Is not the position absurd? Will not the minister give this consideration in order to rectify what is obviously a defect in the act? I appreciate his difficulties, but we must not forget these cases.

I appreciate what my hon. friend says. We are dealing with a difficult proposition. On two occasions the

Thanks very much.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. PETER HEENAN (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 171 to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions-"Labour Union" or "Union"-"Label".

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: On this clause would the minister kindly give us an outline of the intention of the bill so we may save time?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The bill simply gives permission to the labour unions to register their labels. Similar permission is granted in Great Britain and in forty-eight states of the union. But it is provided that no union label may be placed on goods without the authority of their proprietor. Power is given the Exchequer court to cancel the label under certain conditions. The bill also provides that once an employer gets the right to place the label on any of his goods, that right cannot be withdrawn without giving twelve months' notice. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is the judge as to what labels may be registered.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In regard to the twelvemonth notice, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) mentioned to me a few minutes ago that he thinks in some cases this notice is not sufficient. But according to my reading of clause 6, subsection (b) the point is covered. This is the subsection:
A labour union may authorize the use of any label registered by it and such authorization to use shall be subject to cancellation only upon twelve months' notice, unless otherwise speci-IMr. J. H. King.]
fied in any agreement for the use of such label; and any goods may be at any time sold bearing such label, if when such label was used in respect of such goods, the person, firm or corporation was so authorized.
Will the minister tell me if I am correct in this? Suppose a company making a certain line of goods gives permission to the labour union to put on the label, and subsequently the union withdraws the permission, if the company at the end of the year still has some goods on hand so labelled they will be permitted to sell those goods?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The section is intended
to cover that point.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think it does cover it
Apparently my hon. friend did not turn over the page. He is not very strongly in favoui of the bill and had hoped to be here to discuss it. In subsection 3 of section 2 it is provided that the label shall not be placed upon any goods without the consent of the owner or proprietor of such goods. It seems to me that the owner is pretty well protected.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes. The representatives of the employers and the employees met th? Labour department officials and agreed to the bill.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: My interpretation is correct in respect to those two points?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does the label become
a proprietary label just like an ordinary trade mark?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It will, after the bill is
passed.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then this legislation is
really administered by the Department of Trade 'and Commerce?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Is the Minister of Trade
and Commerce alive to what the Minister of Labour is doing? The Minister of Labour is not putting anything over him in the dark in his absence?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour
would not do that.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 7 inclusive agreed to.
On section 8-Suit of proprietor.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Can anyone but a member of a union apply to the Exchequer court for cancellation of registration?

Trade Mark Act

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Nobody but a labour union under the signature of the president or secretary.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
According to that no
other person would have the right of entry to the Exchequer court.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is my understanding of it.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is there any objection to anybody else having that right?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It would not fill the bill
if any person could apply for a labour union lalbel.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This is for cancellation of registration.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I did not catch the question property. Anybody can apply for cancellation.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would the minister be
good enough to show me Where that occurs in the bill?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Section 7 reads:
The Exchequer court of Canada may, on application-[DOT]
It does not say who should apply.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Section 7 which has just been passed, provides that the Exchequer court may, on application, cancel the registration. Then section 8, as I read it, limits the power to apply to the Exchequer court to officers and so forth, of a labour union. But the other party to the'agreement provided for, I think, in section 6, would not have the same right. Would the minister be good enough to explain why the other party to the agreement would not also have the right to apply to the Exchequer court?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I figure that any person would have the right to apply to the Exchequer court for cancellation.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That would appear to
me to be common sense, but I do not see it provided for in this section; indeed, I think the reverse is the case. I had the opinion that the minister really intended that application could be made to the court by either party to the agreement, but section 8 limits that to one side of the agreement, to one party

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
A difficulty arises here.
In the act, section 18, which section 7 of the bill proposes to amend, provides that:
Any person who has registred a trade mark may petition for the cancellation of the same.
And so on. Then subsection (3) of section 7 of this bill provides:
The Exchequer court of Canada may, on application and after investigation and hearing of the parties concerned, direct the cancellation of the registration of any label.
And so on. That would look as if any person could apply for the cancellation of registration of a union trade mark or label, but in the case of a private trade mark only the person who has registered may apply for the cancellation. Is it the intention of the minister that the public at large shall be entitled to apply to the Exchequer court for cancellation, or only the person or union that has registered?

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have not studied that
question, but section 8 does not deal with the question of cancellation at all.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am speaking of section
7. That is where the difficulty arises.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would say that the person who owns the label would be the one who would apply for cancellation.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then section 7 should
be amended to make it conform to the provisions of section 18, which is printed on the opposite page, and which provides that only the person who registers is entitled to apply for cancellation. The language of the bill would imply that any person, including the trade union, can apply to the Exchequer court for cancellation of the trade union label.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Would this meet the difficulty?
The Exchequer court of Canada may, on application by the proprietor of the label

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
On application of the
person or union who has registered the label.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
is right there.

maintopic: TRADE MARK AND DESIGN ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It might be well to let
this go as it is. We have drawn the minister's attention to the possible anomaly. If the minister will give the matter thought, an amendment can be made later, if necessary, in the Senate.

Section agreed to.
Sections 9 and 10 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Canada Grain Act (1925, c. 33) in respect to the issue of warehouse receipts by a private terminal to the shipper or his consignee, and as to the contents of warehouse receipts issued by the person operating any country elevator.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Will the minister explain?

The major feature of this measure is the same as the legislation which was before the House last year in the form of a private bill sponsored by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell). It first saw the light of day in the form of a subsection of a certain section of the original bill of 1925 known as the Turgeon draft bill, but for reasons I do not need to go into, it did not get through the House. Last year the measure did get through this House but became stranded in the Senate, also for reasons which I need not go into.

Yes, there is a very small one, but I forget its nature; it is comparatively unimportant. I believe it is requested by the pools.
